newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Job protests spread as Argentina admits problem.
newsitem.headline: Job protests spread as Argentina admits problem.

text.p: New roadblock protests at Argentina's high unemployment rate spread across the country on Tuesday as Economy Minister Roque Fernandez acknowledged that the government might not be doing enough for the poor.

In the poor northwestern province of Jujuy, where more than 100 people were hurt in clashes last week between police and shanty dwellers picketing a highway, roadblocks cropped up in 10 separate towns.

In the central province of Cordoba, jobless farmhands unhappy with government offers of work programmes and free seeds for planting blocked a highway, while one major access road to the provincial capital was picketed by urban unemployed.

Roadblock protests against an unemployment rate of over 17 percent -- which rises to up to 37 percent in some parts of poor provinces like Jujuy -- have cropped up from the southern reaches of Patagonia to the northern Andes in recent weeks.
President Carlos Menem, whose time in power since 1989 has seen the economy grow but unemployment also rise from just 6 percent, blamed the unrest on "presubversive gymnastics."
But unions blamed it on his privatisations. The Catholic church and even the International Monetary Fund warned him of the dangers of ignoring the poor and jobless.

Economy Minister Fernandez, accompanying Menem on a visit to Germany to boost trade and trumpet the macroeconomic achievements of the Peronist government, also spoke of unrest fanned by politicians ahead of Congress elections in October.
But he told Argentine reporters: "Perhaps we are not doing everything possible, perhaps the resources we have are not being applied in the most efficient manner possible."

Jujuy provincial Gov. Carlos Ferraro faced a strike led by stateworkers' union chief Carlos "the Dog" Santillan," who demanded Ferraro resign for "the savage repression suffered by a people who do not have even their basic needs."

Ferraro in turn blamed the central government for not heeding the problems of the provinces. Jujuy's protesters were demanding 10,000 new jobs, but central government negotiators offered them just 1,500 temporary positions.

A government report published in the press this week showed Jujuy was one of four provinces to have missed out completely on Argentina's "economic miracle." While the economy grew 18.3 percent from 1991-95, Jujuy's shrunk 7.7 percent.
